text: Thomas Ryder (1746–1810), an engraver, studied under James Basire and, during his apprenticeship, submitted drawings to the Society of Artists in 1766 and 1767. He was among the first students at the Royal Academy's schools. Ryder produced a few engravings in the line manner, including "The Politician" (a portrait of Benjamin Franklin) after S. Elmer in 1782, and "Vortigern and Rowena" after A. Kauffman in 1802. However, he is most renowned for his stipple engravings, which are considered some of the finest in their category. These include "The Last Supper" after Benjamin West, "The Murder of James I of Scotland" after Opie, "Prudence and Beauty" after A. Kauffman, nine plates from the large edition of Boydell's "Shakspeare," and others based on designs by Bigg, Bunbury, Cipriani, Cosway, Ryley, and Shelley. He also engraved portraits of Mrs. Damer after Kauffman, Henry Bunbury after Lawrence, Sir William Watson, M.D., after Abbot, and Maria Linley after Westall. His engravings were typically printed in brown ink and sometimes in colour. Ryder had a son with the same name who was also an engraver, and together they created the whole-length portrait of Queen Charlotte after Beechey, which appeared as a front piece in the second volume of Boydell's ‘Shakspeare.’ This article draws from a now-public domain publication: "Ryder, Thomas (1746-1810)" in the Dictionary of National Biography, London: Smith, Elder & Co., 1885–1900.
